stories.title: SIOR’s Aaron Barnard: As CRE Gets More Complicated, the Trusted Advisor Matters More
stories.excerpt: Aaron Barnard, courtesy of SIOR Commercial real estate faces a growing list of challenges, from interest rates and geopolitics to supply-chain disruptions, technology and changing workplace expectations. Those issues will be among the topics discussed when the Society of Industrial and Office REALTORS (SIOR) gathers in New York for its Fall Event Oct. 19-22. The event will bring together CRE professionals from around the world as SIOR celebrates its 85th anniversary. According to incoming global president and Cushman & Wakefield senior director Aaron Barnard, succeeding in the current environment comes down in part to what he calls “relationship intelligence,” a key component of being a trusted advisor. “We’re entering a time where the trusted advisor is more important than ever because of the speed and rate of change,” Barnard told Connect CRE. Artificial Intelligence vs. Relationship Intelligence On the technology side, Barnard sees plenty of uses for artificial intelligence. A professional who gets a lead on a particular company can use AI to research the business, its geography, relevant news and other information. That broker can become “smart enough to be dangerous really fast,” he said, as long as the information is fact-checked. AI is an assistant, not the ultimate authority. Everything still needs to be independently verified before moving ahead. A bigger question is whether AI will replace entry-level brokerage work. “I don’t see it taking away,” Barnard said. “It takes away some of those entry-level jobs, but it changes the entry-level job.” AI could change the nature of what an entry-level broker needs to know. “When I hire a college graduate today, I need to know, first, how motivated they are. The second thing I want to know is if they can write really good prompts or verify data,” Barnard said. bullets: SIOR fall event Oct 19-22 NY draws global CRE professionals amid rising complexity
Aaron Barnard (Cushman & Wakefield) highlights AI as assistant, not replacement for brokers
Trusted advisor relationships increasingly critical as geopolitics, rates, supply chains shift
stories.summary: SIOR's incoming global president Aaron Barnard argues that commercial real estate's mounting headwinds—interest rates, geopolitics, supply-chain disruptions, and changing workplace norms—make relationship intelligence and trusted advisors more valuable than ever. While he sees AI as a tool to help brokers research companies and markets quickly, he emphasizes the technology must be fact-checked and cannot replace human judgment. The shift means entry-level brokerage roles will change but not disappear.
stories.impact: Limited direct impact on multifamily development. This is primarily a message about brokerage and advisory evolution. However, it signals rising complexity in capital sourcing and deal-making environments that developers navigating construction financing, CMBS, and site acquisition will face—expect increased friction and advisory costs in transactional processes.

stories.title: Law Firm Morgan & Morgan Signs 71K-SF Lease at One Seaport Plaza
stories.excerpt: Personal injury law firm Morgan & Morgan has signed a 70,602-square-foot lease at 199 Water Street, also known as One Seaport Plaza, according to third-quarter Manhattan office reports from Colliers and CBRE. Morgan & Morgan will move from a sublease to a long-term direct lease as part of the new deal, according to a source. The law firm moved into the building as a subtenant during the third quarter of 2023, relocating from Midtown and originally taking 34,792 square feet, according to a report issued at the time from the Downtown Alliance. This new lease gives the law firm a more permanent home at Jack Resnick & Sons’ One Seaport Plaza and expands its office footprint. Cushman & Wakefield brokered the deal for both the tenant and the landlord. C&W and Morgan & Morgan did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s requests for comment. The asking rent and the length of the lease were unclear. The average asking rent for office space in Lower Manhattan was $64.88 per square foot during the third quarter of 2026, according to Colliers. However, previous CO reporting noted an asking rent of $40 per square foot in the building. Built in 1984 on Water Street between John and Fulton streets, One Seaport Plaza spans over 1 million square feet, offering amenities that include a cafe and lounge area. Other tenants in the building include fintech firm VCT Holdings, insurance firm Seneca and law firm Foster Garvey. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Morgan & Morgan law firm expands 71K SF lease at 199 Water Street, Lower Manhattan
Firm grows from 34.8K SF sublease (Q3 2023) to 70.6K SF direct lease; moved from Midtown
Lower Manhattan office averaging $64.88/SF Q3 2026; subtenant-to-direct conversion signals stability
stories.summary: Personal injury law firm Morgan & Morgan has expanded and formalized its footprint at Jack Resnick & Sons' One Seaport Plaza, signing a 70,602-square-foot long-term direct lease after initially subleasing 34,792 square feet in Q3 2023. The firm relocated from Midtown Manhattan to Lower Manhattan roughly three years ago. The transaction converts the tenant from a temporary sublease to permanent occupancy, effectively doubling its space, though rent and term length remain undisclosed. Average asking rent in Lower Manhattan is $64.88/SF.
stories.impact: Multifamily developers should note Lower Manhattan's sustained office conversion and repositioning activity. While this is office-focused, the precedent of professional services firms committing long-term to Lower Manhattan—combined with the submarket's lower rents versus Midtown—suggests underlying demand for residential in downtown Manhattan submarkets (Battery Park, Tribeca, DUMBO) may tighten if office-to-residential conversions accelerate or if employer stability (law firms, tech) drives residential demand. Monitor supply constraints in Lower Manhattan residential inventory relative to job concentration.

stories.title: AI Video Platform Synthesia Leases 50K SF for New U.S. Headquarters
stories.excerpt: Lee & Associates NYC announced that Synthesia, an AI video platform for business, has signed a 50,000-square-foot lease at GFP Real Estate’s 675 Ave. of the Americas for its new U.S. headquarters. The company has relocated from 245 Fifth Ave., where it previously occupied approximately 13,000 square feet. Dennis Someck and Justin Myers of Lee & Associates NYC represented Synthesia in the transaction. Jeffrey Gural and Alphie Toro of GFP Real Estate, along with Anthony Sciacca and Scott Gutnick of Newmark, represented the landlord, GFP Real Estate. The lease represents a nearly fourfold expansion of Synthesia’s New York City footprint and is part of a broader U.S. growth strategy. The company has more than 250 employees in the U.S., including approximately 140 in New York, and plans to add more U.S. roles by the end of 2026. “As a fast-growing AI hub, New York is attracting the talent and innovation energy we need to scale,” Laura Gonzalez, chief of staff at Synthesia, wrote in a blog posting. The post AI Video Platform Synthesia Leases 50K SF for New U.S. Headquarters appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Synthesia AI platform leases 50K SF HQ at 675 Ave Americas; nearly 4x footprint expansion NYC

AI hub positioning drives talent attraction strategy; NYC competing as innovation center
stories.summary: AI video platform Synthesia has signed a 50,000-square-foot lease at GFP Real Estate's 675 Avenue of the Americas for its U.S. headquarters, representing a nearly fourfold expansion from its previous 13,000-square-foot footprint at 245 Fifth Avenue. The company employs over 250 people in the U.S., with approximately 140 based in New York, and plans to add more headcount through end of 2026. Leadership cited New York's status as a fast-growing AI hub as central to scaling operations and attracting talent.
stories.impact: Strong signal of tech/AI talent clustering and employer growth in Manhattan core. Synthesia's rapid expansion and deliberate HQ repositioning to Midtown (675 Ave of Americas) signals sustained corporate demand for premium office space that supports recruitment of high-wage tech talent. Multifamily developers should view this as indirect demand driver for workforce housing in Manhattan and nearby transit-connected neighborhoods. Tech-heavy submarkets (Chelsea, Flatiron, Midtown South, Hudson Yards) will see wage-driven rental growth and higher-income tenant demand; consider development near existing or emerging tech corridors.

stories.title: Rockland Trust Provides Financing for Quincy Affordable Development
stories.excerpt: Rockland Trust is providing a financing package of $7.4 million to Father Bill’s & MainSpring (FBMS) for the development of a new 24-unit affordable housing community at 150-156 Quincy St. in Quincy, MA. The Quincy Street Apartments project will transform the site into a multifamily residential community designed to expand access to housing in a region facing significant housing affordability challenges. The project will utilize Low-Income Housing Tax Credits and other public and private funding sources to ensure long-term affordability. Stratford Capital serves as the tax credit syndicator, bringing additional equity investment to support the development. “Father Bill’s has a remarkable track record of creating housing opportunities for individuals and families in need. This project reflects the power of collaboration between nonprofit organizations, public agencies, and financial institutions to address the growing demand for affordable housing across Massachusetts,” said Charles Testa, VP Commercial Banking Officer at Rockland Trust. “Access to affordable housing is essential to building strong, thriving communities.” The post Rockland Trust Provides Financing for Quincy Affordable Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Rockland Trust finances 24-unit affordable housing in Quincy MA with $7.4M; LIHTC structure
Father Bill's & MainSpring (FBMS) nonprofit developer; Stratford Capital syndicates tax credits
Project signals affordable housing demand in Boston-area market facing affordability crisis
stories.summary: Rockland Trust has provided a $7.4 million financing package to Father Bill's & MainSpring for the Quincy Street Apartments, a 24-unit affordable multifamily community in Quincy, Massachusetts. The project utilizes Low-Income Housing Tax Credits and public/private funding to ensure long-term affordability. Stratford Capital serves as the tax credit syndicator, bringing additional equity support.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to market-rate multifamily development. However, the transaction underscores severe affordability constraints in Greater Boston, particularly suburbs like Quincy, which will compress rental upside for market-rate operators and increase regulatory/community pressure for inclusionary zoning. For Trammell Crow Residential considering Boston-area development, this signals: (1) strong LIHTC fund availability and nonprofit density; (2) municipal appetite for affordable units, potentially requiring mixed-income product; (3) continued preference by lenders and syndicators for affordable deals, tightening capital for market-rate projects in the region.

stories.title: City National Bank of Florida Sells Former HQ in Coral Gables After Moving Out
stories.excerpt: After moving across the street earlier this year, City National Bank of Florida has sold its former headquarters in Coral Gables, Fla., for $39 million, property records show. Nonprofit hospital operator Baptist Health South Florida purchased the four-story office building at 2855 South Le Jeune Road, two blocks west of Ponce Circle Park, between Sevilla and Palermo avenues. The 121,418-square-foot building was built in 2007 on a 0.7-acre site. Last year, the bank signed a 144,878-square-foot lease to relocate at 2701 South Le Jeune Road to bring its workforce, which is based in Miami-Dade County, under one roof. Earlier this year, the tenant moved into the 15-story property, which is owned by Zara’s billionaire founder Amancio Ortega. At its former headquarters, City National Bank of Florida first owned the ground-floor space before buying the top-floor office condos for $10 million in 2017, the South Florida Business Journal reported. It’s unclear how Baptist Health South Florida, one of the largest health networks in the region, plans to use the building. It operates a corporate office at 6855 Red Road, near South Miami. Coral Gables, a wealthy suburb next to Miami, has seen an uptick in office sales in recent months. In July, insurance giant PGIM sold a 717,805-square-foot asset for nearly $100 million. In January, Deutsche Bank offloaded 3-acre property for nearly $120 million. A spokesperson for City National Bank of Florida declined to comment. A representative for Baptist Health South Florida did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: City National Bank of Florida sells former 121K SF HQ in Coral Gables for $39M to Baptist Health
Bank relocated to 144.9K SF at 2701 South Le Jeune Road (Amancio Ortega-owned building) in 2026
Office-to-healthcare conversion; Coral Gables office market losing bank anchor; consolidation trend
stories.summary: City National Bank of Florida has sold its former headquarters, a 121,418-square-foot, four-story office building at 2855 South Le Jeune Road in Coral Gables, for $39 million to Baptist Health South Florida. The bank relocated across the street earlier this year to a 144,878-square-foot leased space at 2701 South Le Jeune Road (owned by Amancio Ortega) to consolidate its Miami-Dade workforce under one roof. The Coral Gables property was built in 2007 and sits on 0.7 acres.
stories.impact: Signals corporate consolidation and office-to-healthcare conversion in Miami-Dade County, particularly Coral Gables. For multifamily developers, this indicates: (1) office space being repurposed away from traditional corporate anchor tenants toward healthcare—a structural headwind for office markets in South Florida; (2) healthcare employers (Baptist Health is a major regional network) are consolidating and expanding, creating localized job growth and potential demand for workforce housing near medical campuses; (3) the Coral Gables submarket may see increased supply of conversion-eligible office stock, signaling softness in traditional office but opportunity for adaptive reuse (office-to-residential conversions). Monitor Baptist Health's real estate footprint expansion as a proxy for healthcare job growth in Miami.

For Trammell Crow Residential, this suggests: (1) increased private credit competition and availability for development financing; (2) specialized expertise in CRE finance and leasing is consolidating among elite firms, which may increase advisory costs; (3) New York remains a deep capital markets hub, supporting major development pipelines in the region.

stories.title: Recent Capital Improvements Drive Van Nuys Apartment Deal
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s El Segundo Investment Sales team led by Brent Sprenkle, in collaboration with the firm’s Los Angeles office led by Elliot Hassan and Mike Hanassab, brokered the $5.25-million sale of Vanowen Apartments, a 24-unit low-rise multifamily community located at 15022 Vanowen St. in Van Nuys. The Northmarq team represented the seller, David H. Greenhut. The buyer is The El Camino Trust. “The capital improvements already in place — new roof, upgraded electrical, copper plumbing — meant the buyer could step in with a stabilized asset from day one, and it is exactly why this property sold for the price it got,” Hassan said. Vanowen Apartments presented investors with an opportunity to acquire a well-maintained asset featuring recent capital improvements, according to Northmarq. The community offers one- and two-bedroom apartment homes with onsite laundry facilities, renovated units and upgraded electrical sub-panels. The asset sits on a 0.50-acre parcel and encompasses 27,644 square feet. The post Recent Capital Improvements Drive Van Nuys Apartment Deal appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: 24-unit Vanowen Apartments Van Nuys sold for $5.25M; new roof, upgraded electrical, plumbing
Capital improvements (not new development) drove valuation; buyer El Camino Trust acquired stabilized asset
Northmarq brokered; deal highlights value of deferred maintenance catch-up in LA value-add market
stories.summary: Northmarq's El Segundo team brokered the $5.25 million sale of Vanowen Apartments, a 24-unit low-rise community at 15022 Vanowen Street in Van Nuys, Los Angeles. The seller was David H. Greenhut; buyer is The El Camino Trust. The property features recent capital improvements including a new roof, upgraded electrical systems, copper plumbing, and renovated units. The 0.50-acre community encompasses 27,644 square feet with one- and two-bedroom floor plans and onsite laundry.
stories.impact: This deal signals stabilized, value-add multifamily assets in Los Angeles's San Fernando Valley are in demand despite high construction costs and competitive development environment. The $5.25M sale (or ~$218K per unit for a 24-unit) reflects investor appetite for fully-deferred-maintenance-cured, turnkey portfolios where capex is behind them—suggesting it is cheaper/faster to buy and stabilize existing stock than to develop new in Van Nuys. For Trammell Crow Residential, this implies: (1) LA infill markets favor acquisitions and renovation over ground-up development when construction costs remain elevated; (2) competition for stabilized assets remains fierce; (3) market-rate rental demand in Valley markets is strong enough to justify capex without rent premiums—focus instead on standardized, efficient operations.

stories.title: Westwood Financial Pays $56M for Huntington Beach, Calif., Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: Westwood Financial has bagged a grocery-anchored shopping center in Huntington Beach, Calif., for approximately $56.2 million, adding one of Orange County’s tightly held coastal retail properties to its portfolio. Real estate giant Blackstone sold the 95,416-square-foot Peninsula Marketplace for about $589 per square foot, according to records with PropertyShark. JLL announced the deal Thursday but declined to disclose the name of the seller or the value of the deal. Peninsula Marketplace is 98.8 percent occupied. The property spans 9.5 acres at 19021-19125 Goldenwest Street. The deal reflects investors’ appetite for grocery-anchored retail throughout Southern California, where new supply is limited. Supermarket chain Ralphs is the anchor tenant and has operated at the center for more than 25 years. The tenant roster also includes Planet Fitness, Carl’s Jr. and Rubio’s Coastal Grill. The acquisition is Los Angeles-based Westwood Financial’s largest in Southern California in more than a decade, according to JLL. Westwood owns and operates more than 120 shopping centers nationwide, with a portfolio concentrated in grocery-anchored and service-oriented retail. JLL’s Gleb Lvovich, Geoff Tranchina and Daniel Tyner marketed the property for sale on behalf of the seller. “Grocery-anchored centers in Huntington Beach rarely trade, and investors are prioritizing that combination of daily-needs tenancy, affluent demographics and limited new supply,” Lvovich said. Blackstone took control of Peninsula Marketplace as part of its $4 billion acquisition of Retail Opportunity Investments Corporation in early 2025. That deal gave Blackstone ownership of more than 30 Southern California retail properties, including eight in Orange County. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Westwood Financial acquires Peninsula Marketplace Huntington Beach for $56.2M; 95.4K SF, 98.8% occupied
Grocery-anchored retail (Ralphs 25+ years); $589/SF; Blackstone seller; largest Westwood SoCal deal 10+ years
Orange County coastal retail constrained supply; investors favoring grocery anchors; strong occupancy
stories.summary: Westwood Financial acquired the 95,416-square-foot Peninsula Marketplace shopping center in Huntington Beach, Orange County for approximately $56.2 million, or $589 per square foot. Blackstone sold the property, which is 98.8 percent occupied. Ralphs supermarket is the anchor tenant and has operated at the center for over 25 years; other tenants include Planet Fitness, Carl's Jr., and Rubio's Coastal Grill. The property spans 9.5 acres at 19021-19125 Goldenwest Street. This is Westwood Financial's largest Southern California acquisition in over a decade.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. However, this signals robust investor appetite for grocery-anchored retail in Southern California despite economic headwinds, reflecting flight-to-quality toward defensible, essential-services real estate. For multifamily developers, the underlying dynamic—constrained supply of coastal Orange County real estate and investor capital seeking essential-use assets—may indicate: (1) residential land is similarly constrained and expensive in Orange County coastal markets; (2) alternative-use properties (retail, industrial) are competing aggressively for scarce developable land; (3) multifamily entitlement and zoning remain restrictive in this region, supporting any existing stabilized supply but pressuring new development economics.

stories.title: Private Equity Firm Brenton Point Inks 9K SF at Marx Realty’s 10 Grand Central
stories.excerpt: Marx Realty has signed two new office deals at its 10 Grand Central property totaling 14,000 square feet, the company announced Thursday. In the largest deal, private equity firm Brenton Point Capital Partners will relocate to 10 Grand Central from 900 Third Avenue and occupy 9,000 square feet on the building’s 24th floor at an asking rent of $108 per square foot, according to Marx. Meanwhile, CornerStone, an artificial intelligence-powered human capital management firm currently located at 11 West 42nd Street, will occupy 5,000 square feet on the second floor of 10 Grand Central, at an asking rent of $85 per square foot, Marx said. “These leases reflect the range of top-of-line companies choosing 10 Grand Central and the beautiful experience we offer,” Craig Deitelzweig, CEO of Marx Realty, said in a statement. “Brenton Point and Cornerstone will each benefit from an environment that brings together thoughtful design, highly personalized service and an extensive collection of hospitality-inspired amenities. ” Cornerstone was represented by CBRE’s Josh Pernice and Frederick Fackelmayer. Brenton Point was represented by Owen Reda and Gary Davies, also from CBRE. JLL’s Mitchell Konsker, Thomas Schwartz, Carlee Palmer and Margaux Kelleher represented Marx in both deals. The brokers and tenants did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s requests for comment. The length of each lease was not disclosed. Standing 35 stories high next to Grand Central Terminal, 10 Grand Central takes a hotel-like approach to the office environment, offering tenants concierge services and amenities worthy of a five-star resort. Other tenants at 10 Grand Central include global data intelligence firm Curinos, bank holding company Merchants Bancorp and national business advisory firm Riveron. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Brenton Point Capital Partners leases 9K SF at Marx Realty's 10 Grand Central, 24th floor, $108/SF
CornerStone AI HR firm takes 5K SF on 2nd floor at $85/SF; total 14K SF two-deal announcement
Both firms relocate to Midtown; mixed-use office building with hospitality-inspired amenities drives leasing
stories.summary: Marx Realty announced two office leases at 10 Grand Central totaling 14,000 square feet. Private equity firm Brenton Point Capital Partners will relocate from 900 Third Avenue and occupy 9,000 square feet on the 24th floor at $108 per square foot; AI-powered human capital management firm CornerStone will take 5,000 square feet on the second floor at $85 per square foot, relocating from 11 West 42nd Street. Marx highlighted the building's personalized service, hospitality amenities, and thoughtful design as drivers of leasing momentum.
stories.impact: Signal of sustained office demand in Manhattan, particularly for emerging tech and financial services firms seeking premium, amenity-rich workspace. For multifamily developers, this reinforces: (1) Midtown core remains an employment and talent hub, supporting high-wage residential demand; (2) office flight is selective—premium repositioned buildings (like 10 Grand Central) retain and attract top-tier tenants, while secondary/aging stock deteriorates; (3) private equity and AI firms clustering in Midtown suggests high-earning workforce concentration; target nearby multifamily submarkets (Hudson Yards, Chelsea, Flatiron) for upscale, tech-forward rental product with strong absorption from relocated corporate employees.

stories.title: Global Design Firm Perkins&Will Takes 51K SF at 135 West 18th Street
stories.excerpt: Global design and architecture firm Perkins&Will has inked a 50,680-square-foot lease at 135 West 18th Street, also known as the Altman Building, in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood, Commercial Observer has learned. The firm signed a 15-year lease to relocate from 1250 Broadway, and will occupy the entirety of the second through fifth floors of the Chelsea building, according to landlord broker Newmark. “Perkins&Will’s decision to lease the full office component of the Altman Building reflects continued demand for distinctive, highly functional workplaces in central Manhattan,” Newmark’s Neil Goldmacher, who represented the landlord, said in a statement. “The building combines the character of a historic Chelsea property with the infrastructure, flexibility and collaborative layout required by a leading design firm.” The asking rent was not disclosed, but the average asking rent for office space in Midtown South was $79.57 per square foot during the third quarter of 2026, according to Colliers data. In addition to relocating, Perkins&Will will consolidate its New York City operations to 135 West 18th Street as part of the firm’s recent merger with Architecture Plus Information. The two companies will operate under the Perkins&Will umbrella. Newmark’s Goldmacher, Howard Kesseler, Todd Hershman and Alexander Kesseler represented the landlord, PJ Mechanical, in this lease. Gerry Miovski and Masha Dudelzak from CBRE represented the tenant. CBRE did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Built in 1896 as a carriage house, 135 West 18th Street is a five-story office building and event space. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Perkins&Will signs 50.68K SF lease at 135 West 18th Street (Altman Building) Chelsea, 15-year term
Global design firm relocates from 1250 Broadway; occupies full second through fifth floors in historic building
Chelsea office average ~$79.57/SF Q3 2026; historic property with modern infrastructure attracts design anchor
stories.summary: Perkins&Will, a global design and architecture firm, has signed a 15-year lease for 50,680 square feet at the Altman Building (135 West 18th Street) in Manhattan's Chelsea neighborhood. The firm is relocating from 1250 Broadway and will occupy the entirety of the second through fifth floors. Newmark represented the landlord. The asking rent was not disclosed, but Midtown South average office asking rent was $79.57 per square foot in Q3 2026. Newmark's broker highlighted the building's combination of historic character and modern infrastructure as attractive to the design firm.
stories.impact: Chelsea office market showing selective strength driven by creative/design tenants valuing character buildings with flexibility. For multifamily developers: (1) Chelsea's office-to-residential conversion potential remains high, as historic buildings attract creative tenants but also can be economically adapted to residential; (2) Perkins&Will's long-term commitment (15 years) to Chelsea suggests design/architecture sector growth and job stability in lower Midtown; (3) the submarket's diverse tenant base (law, design, tech, media) supports younger, higher-income residential demand; (4) monitor Chelsea's inventory of similar historic, flexible buildings for acquisition and adaptive reuse into rental housing if office market softens.
